How can there be stability? Why do you not care for me? <gloss>This is a narrative style</gloss> <note>The term "fu" refers to a poetic mode that directly describes events or feelings.</note>


The character <term>mao</term> <gloss>to cover</gloss> is written with the eye radical.
The pronunciation is <term>hao</term> <gloss>using the fanqie phonetic system: hu plus dao</gloss>.
The pronunciation is <term>bao</term>.


◯ O Sun! O Moon! You look down and cover the earth below. But as for that man, he has departed from our love.

How can there be stability? Why does he not repay my kindness? <gloss>This is a narrative style</gloss>

◯ O Sun! O Moon! You come forth from the East. But as for that man, his reputation is without virtue.

How can there be stability? He makes it so I might as well forget him. <gloss>This is a narrative style</gloss>

◯ O Sun! O Moon! From the East you come. O Father! O Mother! You did not nurture me to the end. How can there be stability? His repayment to me does not follow the proper way. <gloss>This is a narrative style. Lady Zhuang Jiang was not reciprocated by Lord Zhuang of Wei. Therefore, she called upon the sun and moon to lament her grievances, and she composed this poem.</gloss>

<gloss>This poem,</gloss> Sun and Moon, consists of four stanzas, each with six lines.

<summary>This page contains the final three stanzas of the poem Sun and Moon from the Odes of Bei, expressing a wife's lament over her husband's neglect and broken promises. Traditional commentary identifies the speaker as Lady Zhuang Jiang of Wei, who appeals to the celestial bodies and her parents regarding her husband's lack of virtue.</summary>
